table.text: Between December 6, 2024, and January 2, 2025, we sampled rental listings posted by private landlords on Germany's largest online rental platform (immobilienscout24.de, as in the original study). Listings were sampled in four cities/regions with a low AfD vote share in the 2024 European election (Aachen, Bielefeld, Braunschweig, Mainz/Wiesbaden; 6.2-10.9%) and five cities with a high AfD vote share (Chemnitz, Dresden, Gelsenkirchen, Halle/Saale, Magdeburg; 20.7-28.2%; national average: 15.9%). As in the original, we excluded listings targeting specific groups, with fewer than two or more than five rooms, or smaller than 50 m²; additionally, listings larger than 200 m², renting above €1,500 per month, more than 20 km from the city center, and--deviating from the original--those posted by companies or restricted to the platform's paid "MieterPlus" tier, which made up the majority of listings in our screening. The final sample consisted of N = 589 listings (low AfD share: n = 290; high AfD share: n = 299), each randomly assigned to one condition of the 2 (ethnicity: German vs. Turkish) × 2 (sexual orientation: heterosexual vs. gay male) between-subjects design. An a priori power analysis for a single chi-square test (α = .05, power = .95, ω = .18) indicated a required N of 402; we targeted 600 inquiries in total. Because each hypothesis compares two of the four conditions, however, the realized n of about 299 per comparison yields a power of .88 for ω = .18.

text.text: In an online field experiment (N = 589 rental listings), we replicated Study 2 of Mazziotta, Zerr, and Rohmann (2015) on ethnicity, sexual orientation, and their intersection as sources of rental discrimination in Germany.
Extending the design, listings were sampled from cities with low versus high vote shares for the radical-right AfD.

Ten years after the original, a Turkish heterosexual couple again received fewer replies (59% vs. 73%) and fewer invitations to viewings (39% vs. 58%) than a German heterosexual couple (ω = .15 and .19).
As in the original, we found no significant discrimination based on sexual orientation and no evidence that holding both minority statuses reduced discrimination.
Ethnic discrimination did not differ significantly between low-and high-AfD-share cities.
Finding a home in Germany has rarely been as difficult as it is today and it is markedly more difficult for some than for others.

In a representative survey, 35% of housing seekers with a migration background reported racist discrimination in the preceding decade, more than twice the overall rate (Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes, 2020).

Germany's National Discrimination and Racism Monitor paints the same picture with behavioral data: in a nationwide correspondence experiment, fictitious applicants with German-sounding names had a 22% probability of being invited to a viewing, compared to 16% for applicants with names from the Middle East, North Africa, and Turkey (DeZIM-Institut, 2025).
Housing access shapes health, social networks, and economic opportunity, and such discrimination has been illegal in Germany since 2006.

Correspondence tests, in which fictitious applicants differing only in signaled group membership inquire about real listings, are regarded as the gold standard for measuring such discrimination (Auspurg et al., 2019; Flage, 2018).

text.text: Meta-analytically, ethnic discrimination appears in nearly all such experiments, although its estimated magnitude has declined over the decades (Auspurg et al., 2019); robust ethnic penalties have also been documented in Germany (Auspurg et al., 2017).

text.text: Two competing predictions exist for doubly stigmatized applicants.
The double-jeopardy account holds that stigmas accumulate, producing the most discrimination for those belonging to two minority groups (Purdie-Vaughns & Eibach, 2008).

text.text: Empirically, both original studies found ethnic discrimination (Study 1: ω = .31 and .32; Study 2: ω = .14 for replies and .11 for invitations, the latter not statistically significant), no significant discrimination based on sexual orientation (ω ≤ .05), and no support for either intersectional prediction: the Turkish gay male couple did not differ significantly from the Turkish heterosexual couple.
A decade later, it is an open question whether this pattern still holds.

Much has changed since the original data collection in 2013/2014: same-sex marriage was legalized in 2017; anti-immigrant sentiment has become far more politically mobilized, most visibly in the electoral rise of the radical-right party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD); and the housing market itself has tightened considerably.

Survey data give no indication, however, that negative attitudes toward Turkish immigrants have become rarer: social distance toward Turkish neighbors in the German General Social Survey (ALLBUS) was unchanged between 1996 and 2016 (Lux & Gülzau, 2022), and in the biennial Mitte studies the share of respondents endorsing manifestly xenophobic statements fluctuated without a downward trend between 2014 (7.3%) and 2024/25 (7.6%; Zick et al., 2025).

text.text: Analogous regional variation is plausible for ethnic discrimination.

We therefore sampled listings from cities with comparatively low versus high AfD vote shares, using vote share as a proxy for the regional prevalence of antiimmigrant and anti-LGBT attitudes, and tested whether this political context moderates discrimination.

Following the original study, we predicted fewer replies and invitations to viewings for the Turkish than for the German heterosexual couple (Hypothesis 1) and for the German gay male than for the German heterosexual couple (Hypothesis 2), and, as in the original intersectionality rationale, less discrimination against the Turkish gay male than against the Turkish heterosexual couple (Hypothesis 3).
As an extension, we predicted stronger discrimination in high-than in low-AfD-share cities (Hypothesis 4).
Between December 6, 2024, and January 2, 2025, we sampled rental listings posted by private landlords on Germany's largest online rental platform (immobilienscout24.de, as in the original study).

Listings were sampled in four cities/regions with a low AfD vote share in the 2024 European election (Aachen, Bielefeld, Braunschweig, Mainz/Wiesbaden; 6.2-10.9%) and five cities with a high AfD vote share (Chemnitz, Dresden, Gelsenkirchen, Halle/Saale, Magdeburg; 20.7-28.2%; national average: 15.9%).

As in the original, we excluded listings targeting specific groups, with fewer than two or more than five rooms, or smaller than 50 m²; additionally, listings larger than 200 m², renting above €1,500 per month, more than 20 km from the city center, and--deviating from the original--those posted by companies or restricted to the platform's paid "MieterPlus" tier, which made up the majority of listings in our screening.
The final sample consisted of N = 589 listings (low AfD share: n = 290; high AfD share: n = 299), each randomly assigned to one condition of the 2 (ethnicity: German vs.
Turkish) × 2 (sexual orientation: heterosexual vs. gay male) between-subjects design.
An a priori power analysis for a single chi-square test (α = .05, power = .95, ω = .18) indicated a required N of 402; we targeted 600 inquiries in total.
Because each hypothesis compares two of the four conditions, however, the realized n of about 299 per comparison yields a power of .88 for ω = .18.

Each landlord received one standardized German-language inquiry (full text in the supplementary material at https://osf.io/j9n7e/overview?view_only=3e1a1363bd6d4161af84e623c02472d5) in which the sender expressed interest in the apartment, described the couple as 36 years old, employed (teaching and IT), non-smoking, and without children or pets, and asked for a viewing.

text.text: Ethnicity was manipulated through common German versus Turkish first and family names (German heterosexual: Noah and Emma Zimmermann; German gay male: Noah and Paul Zimmermann; Turkish heterosexual: Mehmet and Zeynep Yilmaz; Turkish gay male: Mehmet and Yusuf Yilmaz).
The original study had chosen cohort-typical names and pretested the Turkish first names for gender clarity (Christian, Stefanie, and Stefan Schneider; Mehmet, Fatma, and Hasan Yilmaz).
We retained Mehmet Yilmaz and otherwise took first names from current popularity rankings and family names from frequency lists; all names are unambiguously gendered but were not pretested.

Sexual orientation was manipulated by referring to "meine Partnerin" (female partner) versus "mein Partner" (male partner) in the text and by the two signature names, so that, as in the original, the cue rested on two gendered signals.
We replaced the original, somewhat dated Lebensgefährte/Lebensgefährtin with Partner/Partnerin; both terms unambiguously communicate the partner's gender in German.

As in the original study, we coded (a) whether the landlord replied within one week (reply to inquiry) and (b) whether the reply contained an invitation to a viewing or a request to schedule one (invitation to viewing).
Ambiguous replies were coded by group consensus and invitations were declined promptly.

Hypotheses, design, materials, exclusion criteria, sample size, and the chi-square tests followed a written a priori study protocol; its translation and all deviations, with rationale, are in the supplement at https://osf.io/j9n7e/overview?view_only=3e1a1363bd6d4161af84e623c02472d5.

Because such failures are detectable only among repliers, excluding these cases would selectively remove positive responses from the gay-male conditions and bias the orientation estimates.
We therefore report the full sample as the primary analysis and the reduced sample (N = 577) as a sensitivity analysis (not part of the protocol).

Following the original study, Hypotheses 1-3 were tested with six chi-square tests, which we Holm-corrected within this family of six; the protocol had specified correction across all planned tests (see supplement).
Because comparing the significance of separate subgroup tests is not a valid test of an interaction (Gelman & Stern, 2006), we additionally fitted logistic regressions.

text.text: Hypotheses 1-3 were re-estimated as contrasts in a model with ethnicity × orientation and context as predictors, which also yields the ethnicity × orientation interaction (the direct test of the intersectionality hypothesis) and the context main effect; Hypothesis 4 was tested by a likelihood-ratio test of this model against the full ethnicity × orientation × context model.
As a sensitivity analysis, Hypotheses 1-3 were re-estimated with city fixed effects.

text.text: Both effect sizes exceed the protocol's replication criterion (ω ≥ .10).

Contrary to Hypothesis 2, the German gay male couple did not differ significantly from the German heterosexual couple on replies (63% vs. 73%), χ²(1, N = 300) = 3.42, p = .064, ω = .11, or invitations (48% vs. 58%), χ²(1, N = 300) = 3.35, p = .067, ω = .11.

Contrary to Hypothesis 3, the Turkish gay male and the Turkish heterosexual couple did not differ on replies (55% vs. 59%), χ²(1, N = 289) = 0.39, p = .530, ω = .04, or invitations (36% vs. 39%), χ²(1, N = 289) = 0.22, p = .639, ω = .03.

Model-based contrasts led to the same conclusions (Hypothesis 1: OR = 0.52 and 0.45; Hypothesis 2: OR = 0.62 and 0.64; Hypothesis 3: OR = 0.86 and 0.88, for replies and invitations, respectively; 95% confidence intervals in Table S6), and the ethnicity × orientation interaction was nonsignificant, χ²(1, N = 589) = 0.85, p = .355, and χ²(1, N = 589) = 0.93, p = .335 (interaction ORs = 1.38 and 1.39).

text.text: As in the original's exploratory comparison, the Turkish gay male couple also tended to fare worse than the German gay male couple (replies: p = .164; invitations: p = .052).

Regarding Hypothesis 4, the joint likelihoodratio tests of all political-context interaction terms were nonsignificant for replies, χ²(3, N = 589) = 2.42, p = .490, and invitations, χ²(3, N = 589) = 2.37, p = .499.
Unexpectedly, response rates were higher in high-AfD-share cities (reply: OR = 1.44 [1.03, 2.03]; invitation: OR = 1.77 [1.27, 2.47]).

In the sensitivity analysis excluding the twelve misaddressed replies, all conclusions were unchanged; the orientation effects reached nominal but not Holm-corrected significance (ps = .028), which should be interpreted cautiously given the asymmetric nature of the exclusion.
A decade later, the central findings of Mazziotta et al. (2015) replicated closely.

text.text: A Turkish couple was substantially disadvantaged on the German rental market on both indicators, with effect sizes (ω = .15/.19) at least as large as in the original Study 2 (ω = .14/.11).

This result does not fit the meta-analytic trend of declining ethnic discrimination in housing markets (Auspurg et al., 2019), although a single study cannot overturn an average trend and our modified materials preclude a direct estimate of change over time.
text.formatted: This result does not fit the meta-analytic trend of declining ethnic discrimination in housing markets <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Auspurg et al., 2019)</ref>, although a single study cannot overturn an average trend and our modified materials preclude a direct estimate of change over time.

text.text: It converges, however, with the independent, contemporaneous correspondence experiment of the National Discrimination and Racism Monitor, which likewise found substantially fewer invitations for applicants with non-German names (DeZIM-Institut, 2025).
Descriptively, the gap was larger for invitations than for replies.

Because invitations are nested within replies, this pattern is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, screening at a later stage; testing research has located the strongest disadvantage at the later stages of the allocation process (Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes, 2015).
As in both original studies, we found no significant discrimination based on sexual orientation.

The descriptive gap was nevertheless larger than in the original (ω = .11 vs. .04-.05), and the relative risks for German gay versus heterosexual couples (0.86 and 0.82) resemble the meta-analytic risk ratio of about 0.90 for gay male couples (Flage, 2021).
text.formatted: The descriptive gap was nevertheless larger than in the original (ω = .11 vs. .04-.05), and the relative risks for German gay versus heterosexual couples (0.86 and 0.82) resemble the meta-analytic risk ratio of about 0.90 for gay male couples <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Flage, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The 95% confidence interval for the reply difference between German gay and heterosexual couples ranged from -20 to +1 percentage points; the null result is therefore not evidence of absence.
Both the original study and ours signaled sexual orientation subtly (a gendered partner noun and a first name) to preserve ecological validity.
Such a cue may be read through landlords' default heteronormative schema and go unnoticed, all the more so when first names are unfamiliar.

Twelve landlords (eight in the German, four in the Turkish gaymale condition) addressed a gay male couple as "Herr und Frau," so the cue was missed at least by them and plausibly by others; eleven of these replies contained an invitation.
This trade-off makes our orientation estimates (and probably the original ones) conservative; a stronger or verified manipulation is warranted in future work.

As in the original, holding both minority statuses provided no detectable protective effect: the Turkish gay male couple did not differ significantly from the Turkish heterosexual couple and tended to fare worse than the German gay male couple.

Neither double jeopardy nor beneficial stereotype blending is clearly supported; descriptively, ethnicity mattered more than sexual orientation on this market, although our data cannot establish this firmly (in contrast, Schwegman, 2019, found an additional penalty for Black gay male couples in the US).
Our extension yielded no statistically significant evidence that ethnic or orientationbased discrimination depended on regional political context.
Three caveats apply.

First, context was confounded with market conditions: the high-AfD-share cities showed markedly higher response rates, plausibly because their housing markets are less tight and landlords with many inquiries can discriminate at little cost.

Second, context varied between only nine unequally sampled cities, so any other city characteristic is confounded with it (the Hypothesis 1-3 estimates, by contrast, were robust to city fixed effects).

Third, aggregate vote shares are a coarse proxy for the attitudes of the specific landlords contacted, and they refer to the city proper whereas listings within 20 km may extend into surrounding municipalities; neighborhood-level indicators would provide a stronger test.

Beyond the changed stimuli and the added status information, limitations include the data-collection window over the December holidays, which may have lowered response rates; the restriction to private, non-subscription listings on a single platform; a single name set per condition; the new German first names, which are popular today but were uncommon in the applicants' birth cohort; and the possibility that Turkish names signal lower socioeconomic status in addition to ethnicity (Auspurg et al., 2019).

text.text: Future research should examine the later, decisive stages of the allocation process (viewing to contract), where survey and testing evidence locates the strongest disadvantage (Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes, 2015; DeZIM-Institut, 2025).

This replication shows that the core result of Mazziotta et al. (2015) is robust across a decade, different cities, different names, and a modified operationalization of sexual orientation: prospective tenants with Turkish names remain markedly disadvantaged on the German rental market, and we found no evidence that this depended on regional political climate.
